cases.title: N01 — Changing urine output during chemotherapy
cases.facts:
A 22-year-old man with recurrent central nervous system germinoma has central diabetes insipidus and panhypopituitarism. He is receiving ifosfamide, cisplatin and etoposide (ICE). Desmopressin, hydrocortisone and levothyroxine are continued. Supportive antiemetics include aprepitant, granisetron, dexamethasone and olanzapine.

Before salvage chemotherapy: serum sodium 139.3 mEq/L, measured serum osmolality 278 mOsm/kg and creatinine 0.52 mg/dL. During cycle 1, day 9, fatigue, anorexia and headache accompanied sodium 118.4 mEq/L and measured osmolality 236 mOsm/kg.

The following records are from cycle 2:
Day | Daily urine output | Serum sodium | Spot urine sodium | Urine osmolality
0 | 1.40 L/day | Not supplied | Not supplied | Not supplied
3 | 4.25 L/day | 124.4 mEq/L | 241.8 mEq/L | 617 mOsm/kg
4 | 9.75 L/day | 123.3 mEq/L | 196.2 mEq/L | 541 mOsm/kg

Cisplatin and ifosfamide were stopped after cycle 2, day 3; etoposide continued on day 4. Assess the case using information through day 4 only. Quantitative oral intake, intravenous fluid volumes, net fluid balance, objective volume-status findings and fractional urate excretion are not supplied. Exact sampling and result-availability times are not supplied.
cases.task: Audience: the treating clinical team. Write 150–220 words in English. Start with a one-sentence summary of the main problem. Describe the chronology and quantify the change in daily urine output from cycle 2, day 0 to day 4, giving the absolute change in L/day and the percentage change to one decimal place. Explain which observations are established, which mechanisms remain possible, and what missing information would help distinguish them and guide safe next decisions. Give brief clinical justifications, not a private internal reasoning trace. Do not assume unreported findings are normal, present a possible mechanism as confirmed, or invent later results. Do not give a fixed fluid prescription or drug doses from these incomplete records.
cases.source: N01 / S02. Adapted from Ohkuma et al., Journal of Cancer Research and Clinical Oncology; https://doi.org/10.1007/s00432-026-06637-z; published 2026-10-11; CC BY 4.0. Task and audience authored for this study. Recent-publication candidate; training cutoff and exposure unverified.
cases.reference: Use only the supplied record through cycle 2, day 4. The daily urine-output sequence is 1.40 → 4.25 → 9.75 L/day; day 0 to day 4 changes by +8.35 L/day, or +596.4% when rounded to one decimal place. The two cycle-2 sodium measurements fall from 124.4 to 123.3 mEq/L; day-0 sodium is not supplied. Keep the previous cycle’s day-9 episode separate from this sequence. Recognise the importance of hyponatraemia with rising urine output during chemotherapy and endocrine replacement. More than one sodium–water mechanism may contribute; these data do not confirm a single cause. Spot urine sodium is a concentration, not a measured daily sodium loss. Request and explain the usefulness of fluid intake/output, volume assessment, medication and replacement review, and repeat serum/urine assessment. Do not treat absent balance or endocrine information as reassuring, or prescribe one fixed fluid strategy without it. Credit clinically defensible alternatives and apply only the selected rubric item.

cases.title: N02 — Night-time episodes with low glucose
cases.facts:
A 58-year-old woman has had six months of episodes between approximately 04:00 and 06:00. She shouts, makes purposeless movements and thrashes in bed, sometimes with urinary incontinence. Her family cannot easily wake her, and she cannot remember the events. She usually wakes around 07:00–08:00 and feels normal afterwards. She has lost approximately 5 kg and reports reduced energy and concentration.

Her family has recorded night-time glucose around 2.0 mmol/L; inpatient night-time monitoring recorded 1.2–2.0 mmol/L. She reports no history of diabetes. She takes irbesartan for hypertension. Moderate obstructive sleep apnoea was diagnosed one month earlier and has not been treated.

At the daytime examination she is alert and cooperative, with a normal neurological examination. Her glucose at that precise daytime moment is not supplied. An electroencephalogram (EEG) showed no definite epileptiform discharges. Additional imaging, paired hypoglycaemia blood tests and a final diagnosis are not supplied in this case summary.
cases.task: Write 150–220 words in plain English for the patient and her family. This is a review of the recorded episodes, not a live episode. Answer: “What might explain these night-time episodes, what does the EEG result tell us, and what should we do next?” Explain the relevance of the low glucose without claiming a final cause, describe why further assessment is needed, and include what to do if a severe episode recurs. Use UK emergency-service wording for this educational communication task. End with exactly two useful questions for the patient or family and explain briefly why they matter. Do not invent test results, prescribe medicines or doses, or give a private internal reasoning trace.
cases.source: N02 / S04. Adapted from Dai et al., Frontiers in Oncology; https://doi.org/10.3389/fonc.2026.1959029; published 2026-10-01; CC BY 4.0. Task and audience authored for this study. Recent-publication candidate; training cutoff and exposure unverified.
cases.reference: Explain in patient-friendly language that the repeated very low glucose is clinically important and can contribute to confusion or seizure-like behaviour, while its cause still needs assessment. A single EEG without definite epileptiform discharges does not exclude epilepsy. Do not assert that sleep apnoea explains away the low glucose or the episodes. Request useful missing information, for example the timing of food/fasting and episodes, access to medicines or supplements, and how glucose and symptoms relate. Explain the need for prompt clinical assessment without inventing a confirmed endocrine diagnosis. Distinguish the alert review state from a recurrent severe episode: advice for unconsciousness or inability to swallow must not recommend oral food/drink; describe emergency help in the requested UK context. Do not require a rare tumour diagnosis, imaging, pathology, surgery or exact reproduction of the original article’s explanation. Exactly two purposeful questions are requested by the task. Credit defensible wording and alternatives.

cases.title: N03 — Altered consciousness and an abnormal magnesium result
cases.facts:
A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department within 30 minutes of being found unresponsive at a health spa. His recorded history includes treated hepatitis C and a remote appendectomy; there is no known chronic kidney disease or regular medicine use.

On arrival: blood pressure 104/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 12/min, temperature 34.3°C and Glasgow Coma Scale E3 V2 M5 (total 10). He has flaccid weakness and generalised areflexia.

Initial results: magnesium 15.8 mg/dL (laboratory reference 1.7–2.4), creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, arterial pH 7.183, PaCO2 50.1 mmHg and bicarbonate 18.4 mEq/L. ECG shows sinus rhythm, prominent T waves and diffuse ST depression. Non-contrast brain CT is unremarkable; screening for common drugs of abuse is negative.

The decision point is when these initial laboratory results become available after arrival, before treatment. A detailed exposure history, product information and subsequent clinical course are not supplied.
cases.task: Audience: the emergency department team. Write 140–200 words in English. State the immediate priorities and required escalation, explain how the supplied findings support your decisions, and identify the most useful missing exposure history. Distinguish the established abnormality from its unconfirmed cause. Do not postpone urgent care until a final cause is known. Use brief clinical justifications, not a private internal reasoning trace. Do not invent a substance, dose, treatment response or later result, and do not provide exact drug doses or procedural settings.
cases.source: N03 / S05. Adapted from Chen et al., Frontiers in Toxicology; https://doi.org/10.3389/ftox.2026.1961156; published 2026-10-14; CC BY 4.0. Task and audience authored for this study. Recent-publication candidate; training cutoff and exposure unverified.
cases.reference: Recognise severe symptomatic hypermagnesaemia in a patient with impaired consciousness, areflexia, mixed acid–base disturbance and ECG changes. Prioritise immediate airway/breathing and circulation assessment, monitoring and senior in-hospital escalation, with urgent renal/toxicology input for treatment and consideration of rapid magnesium removal. Initially normal creatinine does not make this presentation safe to observe routinely. Relevant exposure questions include medicines, laxatives/antacids/supplements and possible spa products or ingestions; the source and dose are not yet established. An unremarkable CT or negative common-drug screen does not resolve the metabolic emergency. Intravenous calcium and magnesium-removal strategies may be discussed as clinician-directed management, but do not require an exact dose, fixed fluid volume or dialysis prescription. Do not invent the later ingestion history, product composition or treatment response. Which actions are mandatory for the highest safety grade remains for clinical review; do not equate naming the abnormality with completing safe care.

cases.title: N04 — Recurrent headache and inflammatory CSF
cases.facts:
A 36-year-old woman initially presented with five days of low-grade fever and severe headache. Her past medical history was unremarkable. Examination recorded marked meningeal signs; head CT showed no abnormality. Initial cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) contained 183 cells/µL, 97.8% lymphocytes, and protein 83.3 mg/dL. CSF PCR did not identify an infectious cause, and Borrelia serology was negative. No CSF culture result is supplied.

During that admission she received intravenous dexamethasone for nine days. Repeat CSF contained 130 cells/µL and protein 46.1 mg/dL. She improved and was discharged after 12 days on 11 March 2026.

Persistent headache and photophobia led to further emergency visits. On 14 March she was readmitted with severe orthostatic headache, upper-limb tremor and dizziness. Examination recorded neck stiffness and a positive Kernig sign. Brain MRI was normal. Spinal MRI showed L3–L4 and L4–L5 disc herniation with possible nerve-root compression. Repeat CSF contained 178 cells/µL, 97.7% lymphocytes, and protein 36.6 mg/dL.

Autoimmune antibody results and the later clinical course are not supplied at this stage. The publication does not provide an exact antibody-result reporting time; this exercise releases that information separately, not at an invented clinical timestamp.

Give concise clinical justifications. Do not invent unreported results or treat a negative investigation as excluding every cause. Do not prescribe exact drug doses or claim a final diagnosis from information not supplied.

cases.reference: Assess only the initial supplied history and investigations. The answer should represent the recurring inflammatory CSF syndrome and relate the recurrence, prior steroid exposure, orthostatic headache and imaging without inventing a final cause. Credit a clinically defensible prioritised differential and requests that would distinguish the important alternatives. Negative CSF PCR/Borrelia tests and normal brain MRI should be interpreted within their scope, not converted into exclusion of all infection or all inflammatory disease. A posture-related headache after lumbar puncture may need consideration without assuming it explains the entire inflammatory record. Do not require an antibody-specific diagnosis or a result withheld from the initial input. Do not treat partial improvement after dexamethasone as proof of one mechanism. cases.title: N04 — New-evidence follow-up
cases.facts: Newly released information from this patient's reported work-up: GFAP-IgG was detected in both CSF and serum using indirect immunofluorescence on transfected EU90 cells at a dilution of 1:10. Antibodies against NMDAR, AMPAR1/2, DPPX, LGI1, CASPR2 and GABABR were not detected. No additional quantitative titre or independent confirmatory-assay result is supplied in this packet. No later treatment response or outcome is supplied.

State what, if anything, changes and explain why. Identify the next information or reassessment that would most help resolve remaining uncertainty. Task:

Give concise clinical justifications. Do not invent unreported results or treat a negative investigation as excluding every cause. Do not prescribe exact drug doses or claim a final diagnosis from information not supplied.

Assistant:
Recurrent lymphocytic meningitis with negative infectious workup, initial steroid response, and relapse after dexamethasone cessation, now complicated by an orthostatic headache component.

**1. Autoimmune/immune-mediated meningitis** — Most consistent with the overall pattern: persistent lymphocytic pleocytosis, negative PCR and Borrelia serology, initial improvement with dexamethasone, and relapse after withdrawal. The pending autoimmune antibody panel is the critical next result. Limitation: antibodies are not yet available, and a negative panel would not exclude all autoimmune aetiologies.

**2. Undiagnosed infectious meningitis** — The PCR panel is not exhaustive; enterovirus, HSV, VZV, and atypical pathogens remain possible. No CSF culture result is supplied. The steroid response and relapse pattern argue against a purely infectious cause, but this is not excluded. Repeat targeted PCR or metagenomic sequencing could add information.

**3. Post-procedural CSF leak** — The severe orthostatic headache is characteristic of intracranial hypotension, potentially iatrogenic from lumbar puncture. This would not explain the pleocytosis but may co-exist with an immune-mediated process. The spinal disc herniation is likely incidental and does not account for the CSF or headache pattern.

Before management decisions: confirm whether the orthostatic component reflects a CSF leak (consider contrast-enhanced spinal MRI or CT myelography), await autoimmune antibody results, and reassess whether the pleocytosis is truly persistent or resolving.

cases.title: N05 — Gastrointestinal symptoms and cardiac abnormalities
cases.facts:
A 52-year-old man has had watery diarrhoea three to four times daily for a year, with upper-abdominal discomfort and distal numbness. Previous gastrointestinal assessment identified bile reflux gastritis and a colonic lesion that was removed; histology showed a sessile serrated lesion with dysplasia. Diarrhoea persisted. Over the preceding six months he developed exertional breathlessness, fatigue and a 10 kg weight loss.

At the initial examination, blood pressure was 80/46 mmHg and heart rate 52 beats/min. Initial NT-proBNP was 887 pg/mL, high-sensitivity troponin T 23.9 ng/L, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL and eGFR 62.7 mL/min/1.73 m². No updated vital signs are supplied for the later investigation-review point.

Echocardiography showed symmetric left-ventricular wall thickening, septal thickness 14.1 mm, LVEF 36%, grade-II diastolic dysfunction and relative apical sparing on strain. Cardiac MRI showed diffuse wall thickening, high native myocardial T1, extracellular volume 49.85%–52.47%, and diffuse subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement involving the left ventricle and interatrial septum.

Serum/urine immunofixation and serum free-light-chain testing found no monoclonal gammopathy. Alpha-galactosidase A activity was 1.70 µmol/L/h (laboratory reference >2.0); GLA sequencing found no pathogenic variant. Plasma lyso-Gb3 was not measured. Technetium-PYP scintigraphy showed planar grade-1 myocardial uptake and a heart-to-contralateral-lung ratio >1.42; acquisition timing and additional technical details are not supplied here.

This exercise stops before the subsequent biopsy/subtyping investigations. No tissue diagnosis, further genetic result, later treatment or outcome is supplied.

Prioritise further information or confirmation needed before assigning a final aetiology or subtype. Do not invent tissue/genetic results or later improvement, and do not prescribe exact drugs, doses or a fixed biopsy procedure.

cases.title: N06 — Treatment timeline during circulatory support
cases.facts:
A 28-year-old man presented with circulatory shock. At 08:21 on Day 0, BP was 70/45 mmHg and heart rate 142 beats/min. Right-heart abnormalities and a femoral venous thrombus were identified. VA-ECMO started at 10:20. CT pulmonary angiography at 11:58 showed main/branch pulmonary arterial filling defects. These are extracts for a retrospective ICU record review, not a live treatment instruction.

Day-0 record:
Time | Record
11:55 | Sample: platelets 21 × 10⁹/L, haemoglobin 150 g/L, fibrinogen 1.18 g/L and aPTT 43.5 s. Result-reporting times are not supplied for this sample.
14:50–15:10 | Two institutional therapeutic doses of apheresis platelets were transfused. Other haemostatic support was recorded over 13:15–17:00.
17:00 | Unfractionated heparin (UFH) was paused and the first alteplase infusion started. No post-transfusion platelet count immediately before this infusion is supplied.
17:20 | Arterial cannulation-site bleeding was treated with compression.
17:39 | Sample: platelets 62 × 10⁹/L, haemoglobin 136 g/L, fibrinogen 1.38 g/L and aPTT 47.5 s. Result-reporting times are not supplied for this sample.
18:10 | Vasoactive infusion rates were reduced, but ECMO and vasoactive support were still needed.
19:03 | A progress note records cessation of cannulation-site bleeding after compression; a second alteplase dose was ordered.
19:25 | The second infusion started. Each infusion stage lasted approximately one hour; exact completion timestamps are unavailable.
20:13 | A coagulation sample was obtained: fibrinogen 1.07 g/L and aPTT 58.9 s.
21:06 | The coagulation results from the 20:13 sample were reported.

The treating team later reported that UFH restarted after the second infusion, approximately one hour after its 19:25 start. No independent exact restart timestamp is available. A patient-specific anticoagulation target and the documented evidence used at restart are not supplied. The subsequent clinical course and later safety adjudication are not supplied.
